summary: Describes extensions to the Simple Mode of Facsimile Using Internet Mail, adding features such as higher resolution, color, and confirmation of delivery and processing.

plainLanguage.summary: Faxing a page by email is already possible, but the basic version gives no confirmation and sends only low quality images. This document adds two things: a way to be told that the message was delivered and a way to be told that it was printed, and a way to send higher resolution or colour pages when the receiving device says it can handle them.

subtitle: How to fax by email with delivery confirmation, processing confirmation and better quality images.

tldr.problem: Sending a fax as an email message works, but the basic version sends only a low quality image and gives the sender no confirmation that the message arrived or that anything was printed.
tldr.mechanism: The document splits confirmation into two: a Delivery Status Notification confirms delivery to the mailbox, and a Message Disposition Notification confirms processing. It also defines how a sender learns the recipient's capabilities and sends a higher quality TIFF when the recipient supports it.
tldr.outcome: The document standardizes delivery confirmation as required and the additional document features as optional. It extends, rather than replaces, the Simple Mode of Facsimile Using Internet Mail.

facts.label: Confirmation mechanisms
facts.value: Delivery Status Notification and Message Disposition Notification

today: RFC 2532 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It extends the Simple Mode of Facsimile Using Internet Mail in RFC 2305 rather than replacing it.

sections.title: What the Document Adds
sections.content:
This document describes extensions to Simple Mode of Facsimile Using Internet Mail, and additional features including transmission of enhanced document characteristics such as higher resolution and colour, and confirmation of delivery and processing.

The features are designed to give the highest level of interoperability with the existing and future standards-compliant email infrastructure and mail user agents, while providing a level of service close to the one fax users currently enjoy. The enhancements use the existing messaging infrastructure where possible, rather than creating fax-specific features that are unlikely to be implemented in non-fax messaging software.

The document standardizes two features: delivery confirmation, which is required, and additional document features, which are optional. Both are described in full in the companion document on terminology and goals for Internet fax.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending a fax by email works, but the basic version sends only a low quality image and gives no confirmation at all. This document adds confirmation and higher quality images, using the mail system you already have rather than adding fax-only features.

sections.title: The Terms Used
sections.content:
Processing indicates the action of rendering or transmitting the contents of the message to a printer, a display device or a fax machine. A processing confirmation is an indication by the recipient of a message that it is able to process the contents of that message.

The recipient is the device that performs the processing function. For example, a recipient could be implemented as a traditional mail user agent on a PC, a standalone device that retrieves mail using POP3 or IMAP, or an SMTP server that prints incoming messages, similar to an LPR server.

The behaviour of gateways from telephone-network fax to SMTP, called onramps, and from SMTP to telephone-network fax, called offramps, is not described in this document. Such gateways should nevertheless have the behaviour characteristics of senders and recipients as described here.
sections.plainLanguage: Processing means putting the message onto paper, a screen or a fax machine. The recipient is whatever does that: a mail program on a computer, a device that collects mail, or a mail server that prints what arrives.

sections.title: Delivery and Processing Confirmation
sections.content:
In traditional telephone-network facsimile, the receiving terminal acknowledges successful receipt and processing of every page. In Internet mail, the operations of delivery to the mailbox and disposition to paper or a screen may be separated in time, because messages are stored and forwarded, and in location, because the delivery agent and the user agent are separate. The confirmation of these two operations is supplied by two different standards-track mechanisms: Delivery Status Notifications for delivery and Message Disposition Notifications for disposition.

The document sets out the requirements for devices and services that are to be considered compliant with it: what a sender must do, what a recipient must do, and what the mail infrastructure in between must provide.
sections.plainLanguage: On the telephone network a fax machine confirms every page it prints. Email splits that into two steps that can happen at different times and in different places: delivery to the mailbox, and then the message being put in front of a person or a printer. The first is confirmed with a delivery status notification, the second with a message disposition notification.

sections.title: What Senders and Recipients Must Do
sections.content:
Because delivery failure may occur, over disk quota, because the user no longer exists, or because of a misconfigured mailer, a delivery failure message may be sent to the envelope-from address the sender supplied. That address must therefore be able to handle such messages.

If the sender wants delivery confirmation it must request a Delivery Status Notification by including the esmtp-keyword NOTIFY with the esmtp-value SUCCESS. If the sender wants processing confirmation it must request a Message Disposition Notification when sending the message itself. Because a recipient may silently ignore a request for an MDN at any time, MDNs must not be used for delivery confirmation and are only useful for disposition notification, and the sender must not assume the recipient will respond to an MDN request in a later message even if it has done so in the past. The address given in the Disposition-Notification-To field must be able to receive MDNs and should be able to receive messages that are not in the MDN format, because legacy systems generate such responses. That address and the envelope-from address should match, so that automated responses to MDN requests work.

Recipients should implement Message Disposition Notifications and should indicate the media features they support in DSN and MDN messages. A recipient must be configurable to silently ignore a request for an MDN. If the recipient is an automated message processing system with no person behind it, the device may be configurable to always respond to MDN requests, but in all cases must be configurable never to generate MDNs. A recipient must not generate an unsolicited MDN to indicate successful processing, and may generate an unsolicited MDN to the envelope-from address to indicate processing failure, subject to the requirement that an operator must always be able to disable unsolicited MDN generation.

A recipient that uses POP3 or IMAP4 to retrieve its mail must not generate a Delivery Status Notification message, because such a notification, if it was requested, would already have been issued by the delivery agent on delivery to the message store. It must not use the To, Cc, Bcc or other recipient header fields to determine the ultimate destination mailbox, and should not use other RFC822 or MIME fields for that either.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender asks for a delivery report by asking the mail system for it, and for a processing report by putting the request in the message. The receiver may ignore either request at any time, so the sender must not treat a missing report as a failure. A receiver must never send an unsolicited report saying everything worked, but it may send one saying it failed.

sections.title: Messaging Infrastructure Requirements
sections.content:
The SMTP messaging infrastructure used by the sender and the receiver is commonly provided by the internet service provider or a company's internal mailers, but it can be provided by another organisation with the appropriate service contracts.

Support for DSN must be provided by the mail submission server used by the sender, and must be provided up to the mailer responsible for communicating with external mailers.

Support for DSN must be provided by the external, internet-accessible mailer, and must be provided by each mailer between that external mailer and the recipient. If the recipient is implemented as an SMTP server it must also support DSN.
sections.plainLanguage: The mail servers in between have to support delivery reports. That means the server the sender submits to, every server along the way, and the receiving server if that is where the printing happens.

sections.title: Additional Document Capabilities
sections.content:
The base facsimile specification allows sending only the minimum subset of TIFF for Facsimile, unless the sender has prior knowledge of other TIFF fields or values the recipient supports. A recipient may support any or all of the TIFF profiles defined in RFC 2301 in addition to profile S, and should indicate this support, so a sender may use those additional profiles when sending to a recipient with the corresponding capabilities. A sender should be able to recognise and process the feature tags when reviewing the capabilities a potential recipient presents. The capability matching rules allow new features to be introduced that older implementations do not recognise.

A sender may send a message containing both the minimum subset of TIFF for Facsimile and a higher quality TIFF using multipart/alternative.

Three methods for acquiring the recipient's capabilities are described: sender manual configuration; capabilities held in a directory; and capabilities returned in an MDN or DSN. The third method should be used, because it needs no additional infrastructure and the information is acquired automatically. An implementation may cache capabilities locally and lose synchronisation with the recipient's actual capabilities, so a mechanism should let the sender override the local cache.

In manual configuration, the user controlling the sender overrides the default settings, usually per recipient, for example indicating that the recipient can receive high resolution or colour images. The document notes that while this is awkward and not automatic, it reflects the current state of deployment of extended capability configuration for ordinary internet email users.

A future direction is a directory structure of recipient capabilities, deployed for example through LDAP or DNS, so that a sender could determine a recipient's capabilities before constructing or transmitting a message, using a directory lookup. Such mechanisms are not defined in this document, though there is active investigation within the IETF into a solution to the problem. If the recipient implements the capability-reporting specification, the DSN or MDN it returns can contain information describing the recipient's capabilities, which the sender can use for subsequent communications with that recipient.

A sender must not send a message with no processable content to try to elicit a capability response, because that confuses a recipient not already designed to understand such a message. A recipient should indicate the profiles and features it supports even if it supports only Tiff Profile S, so that a sender can determine that the recipient is compliant with this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender needs to know whether the receiving device can handle a better image. The document prefers learning this from the reply to an earlier message, because that needs no extra setup and happens automatically. Manually telling the sender is also allowed, and a shared directory of capabilities is described as a future possibility.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the document extends the base facsimile specification, the security considerations of that specification apply here as well.

Inaccurate capability information could cause a denial of service. The information could be inaccurate for many reasons, including a compromised or improperly configured directory server, improper manual configuration of the sender, compromised DNS, or a spoofed MDN. If a sender is using cached capability information, there should be a mechanism to allow the cached information to be ignored or overridden if necessary.

Forged DSNs or MDNs can provide incorrect information to a sender.
sections.plainLanguage: Two risks stand out. The record of what the receiving device can do may be wrong or tampered with, which can break the sender. And a delivery or processing report can be forged, so the sender should not take it at face value.

sections.title: Implementation Notes
sections.content:
Where the generally available submission server does not support DSNs, it may be useful for the sender to implement mail routing as well as additional submission server functions, so that the installation is not constrained by the limitations of the incumbent submission server.

To provide a high degree of reliability, it is desirable for the sender to know that a recipient could not process a message, and the inability to process a message may be detectable by the recipient's delivery agent or user agent. If the delivery agent determines that the message cannot be processed, it is strongly encouraged to reject the message with a status code of 5.6.1. That status code may be returned in response to the end-of-mail-data indicator if the mailer supports reporting of enhanced error codes, or after message reception by generating a delivery failure DSN.

Providing this functionality in the delivery agent, by either of those two mechanisms, is superior to providing it using MDNs, because MDNs must generally be requested by the sender and the request may at any time be ignored by the receiver. Message rejection performed by the delivery agent can always occur without the sender requesting such behaviour and without the receiver circumventing it.

If the message contains an MDN request and the recipient's user agent determines that the message cannot be processed, the user agent is strongly encouraged to respond to the MDN request and indicate that processing failed, with the disposition-type processed or displayed and the disposition-modifier error or warning.
sections.plainLanguage: If the mail server the sender uses cannot send delivery reports, the sender can add that itself. And if a receiving system knows it cannot print a message, it is better to reject the message at the mail server than to report the failure afterwards, because the sender never has to ask for that.
